title: Good and Bad in Greek: eu- and dys-
short: eu- means good or well and dys- means bad or difficult, in words from Greek.
trouble: Learners confuse eulogy (praise) with elegy (a sad poem). eu- is a clue only at the start of a word.

blocks.html: Greek had its own pair for good and bad. eu- means “good” or “well,” and dys- means “bad” or “difficult.” You may know dysfunction (working badly). These parts are fewer than bene- and mal-, but the words they build show up often in reading.

blocks.html: eu- = good, well. dys- = bad, difficult. Both are Greek and both come at the very start of a word.

Three eu- words are on the list. A euphemism is a mild word in place of a harsh one: eu- (good) + pheme (speech), “speaking well” of something unpleasant. A eulogy is “good words” (eu- + log, word), a speech of praise. Euphoric comes from a Greek word for “bearing well”: so happy you feel you could carry anything.

mn.cue: EU = GOOD: a nice word for a bad thing
mn.text: Grandpa Gus calls his rusty, smoking old car “a classic.” That kind word for a wreck is a {euphemism}.

blocks.cap: A word from the list: euphemism.

blocks.html: Mixing up eulogy and elegy. A eulogy (eu-, good) is a speech of praise, often given at a funeral. An elegy is a sad poem; it has no eu-. And eu- is a clue only at the start of a word: the e-u inside feud or neutral is not this part.

A word pair to know: a dystopia (dys-, bad + top, place) is an imagined society where life is miserable. Its opposite is a utopia, an imagined perfect society. That name was made from Greek words meaning “no place,” a hint that such a perfect place may not exist.
